parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 11. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man talking to the coordinator of a baking club. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 4. Helen: Hello, Riverside Baking Club, Helen speaking. Tom: Oh, hello. My name's Tom Ashworth, and I'd like to join the club. Helen: That's great, Tom. I can take your details over the phone now, if you like, and you can ask me any questions at the same time. Tom: Yes, that would be perfect. Helen: Lovely. It will only take a few minutes. Tom: No problem. I have got plenty of time this morning, and I have been meaning to call for weeks. Helen: So, first of all, what's your address? Tom: It's fourteen Kelsall Road, in Northfield. Helen: Could you spell the name of the road for me? Tom: Yes, it's K, E, L, S, A, L, L. Helen: Thanks. And how did you hear about us? Did you find our website? Tom: I usually find things online, but this time it was my neighbour who told me about you. She came to one of your open days last year and loved it. Helen: Oh, that's nice to hear. And what are you hoping to get out of the club? Tom: Well, I'd really like to enter some of your competitions. I've entered a few before, at other clubs. But mainly I want to learn from people who've been baking for a lot longer than me. I've taught myself most of what I know from videos. Helen: You'll certainly be able to do that. Some of our members have been baking for fifty years! Now, what kind of membership would you like? A single membership is twenty-five pounds a year, and a joint membership for two people is forty pounds. Tom: My wife's keen to come too, actually, so I'll go for the joint membership. Helen: Good choice. Joint members can both vote at the annual meeting, and you both get a discount on our classes. Tom: That sounds good. How often does the club meet? Helen: We meet once a month in the church hall, usually for a demonstration by one of our members, and we hold four competitions a year. There's also a summer fair where members sell their cakes to raise money for charity. Tom: We'd definitely be interested in helping with that. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10. Helen: You mentioned you've entered some competitions before. Could you tell me a bit about them? It helps us to know what level you're at. Tom: Sure. The first one was called Afternoon Tea. You had to produce three different items that would go together on a plate: a cake, a biscuit and something savoury. Helen: That sounds like a lovely theme. What did you make? Tom: A lemon cake, some shortbread and a little cheese tart. I didn't win, but the judges gave me some feedback. They said the pastry on the tart was too heavy. Helen: Ah, that's a common problem. And the second one? Tom: That was a bread competition. The rules said you could make any kind of loaf, but it had to include local honey. There's a beekeeper near us, so that was easy to get hold of. Helen: And how did that go? Tom: Better, I thought. The loaf rose well and tasted good. But the judges said the oven temperature was wrong, because the crust was much too dark. Helen: That's easy to fix with practice. What was the third competition? Tom: It was called Party Pieces. You had to make small cakes or biscuits for a children's party, and there was one important rule: they had to contain no nuts, because of allergies. Helen: Very sensible. What did the judges think? Tom: They liked the decoration, but they said my cupcakes were too sweet for young children. I think I got a bit carried away with the icing. Helen: Well, Tom, it sounds as though you've got plenty of enthusiasm, and we'd be very happy to have you both. Our next meeting is on the first Tuesday of the month. Tom: Is there anything we need to bring to the first meeting? Helen: Just yourselves, and an apron if you'd like to join in the demonstration. We provide all the ingredients, and there's always plenty of tea. Tom: Great, thanks. We'll see you then. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear an expert on wild camping called Ollie Grant talking on a radio programme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Presenter: This evening, I'm delighted to welcome Ollie Grant, who has just written a book about wild camping, that is, camping in the countryside away from official campsites. Ollie, what do people need to know before they try it? Ollie: Thank you. Well, I always start with safety. Wild camping is a wonderful experience, but you need to know what you're doing. The most common mistake I see is people putting their tent up right next to a river or stream, because it looks beautiful. But after heavy rain in the hills, water levels can rise very quickly, even during the night, so you should always camp well above the water. I've been camping in the mountains for over twenty years, and I've seen people get into trouble simply because they didn't think ahead. Ollie: The other thing I'd warn people about is relying on your phone to find your way. The battery can run out, and in the mountains there's often no signal, so always carry a paper map and a compass, and know how to use them. People sometimes ask whether they should camp alone. If you're experienced, I think that's fine, but you must tell someone where you're going. Ollie: There are also a lot of myths about wild camping. Many people believe you need expensive equipment, but that isn't true. You can start with fairly basic gear. What does matter is keeping warm, and here's something that surprises people: if you're cold at night, it's usually not because your sleeping bag isn't warm enough, but because you haven't got a good enough mat underneath you. The cold ground takes the heat from your body. Ollie: People also ask me whether wild camping is legal. The rules vary, but it is permitted in some parts of the country, such as large areas of Scotland, as long as you follow the guidelines. And please don't cook inside your tent, whatever the weather. It's very dangerous. Finally, a lot of people worry about animals attacking their tent at night. That's extremely unlikely. The worst you'll probably get is a curious sheep. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Ollie: Choosing where to camp is really important. People often tell you to look for a sheltered spot, or to avoid valleys, and there's some truth in that. But the most important thing, in my view, is to arrive at your site well before dark, so you can see the ground properly and choose a flat, dry place for your tent. Ollie: If you're a complete beginner, I wouldn't recommend relying on a guidebook, even mine, or on the camping apps you can download. The best way to start is to go on an organised trip with an experienced leader. You'll learn far more that way, and you'll be safe. Ollie: Wild camping depends on leaving the countryside exactly as you found it. You should never light a fire unless it's clearly allowed, and you must take all of your rubbish home with you, including food waste like banana skins, which take a surprisingly long time to break down. Ollie: Sadly, some popular areas have now introduced restrictions on wild camping. That isn't because of the risk of fires, although that is a concern, and it isn't to protect nesting birds. The main reason is that the number of people visiting these areas has increased enormously in recent years, and the damage caused by so many tents has become a real problem. Ollie: A word about storing food. Foxes and even cows can be surprisingly interested in your supplies, so keep your food in a sealed box outside the tent, rather than inside where you're sleeping. And never leave it lying around in open bags. Ollie: Finally, once you've got some experience, do explore new areas. But before you set off, plan your route carefully on a map, so you know where you can find water and how to get back quickly if the weather changes. Right, I'd now like to talk about some of my favourite places to camp. Some of my best memories are of places I'd never heard of until I looked closely at a map. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Anya and Marcus, discussing a seminar on the history of shopping and the future of the high street. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Marcus: That seminar on the history of shopping was really interesting, wasn't it? I'd never thought about how recent some of the things we take for granted are. Anya: I know. I didn't realise that the first self-service grocery store only opened in 1916. Before that, you had to ask a shop assistant for everything, and they'd fetch it from behind the counter. Marcus: Yes, and it completely changed the relationship between customers and shopkeepers. Suddenly people could pick things up, look at them and compare prices themselves. Anya: Exactly. And it's not surprising the idea caught on so quickly. It was faster for customers, and the shops needed fewer staff, so prices came down. Marcus: True. I thought the lecturer was a bit unfair, though, when she said they were the start of the decline of the traditional high street. Anya: Maybe. Anyway, the second half, about the future of shopping, was very optimistic, wasn't it? Marcus: Too optimistic, I'd say. She claimed that within ten years almost all shopping will be done online. I just can't see that. People still enjoy going to the shops, especially for clothes. Anya: I agree. And that idea of most deliveries being made by drones in the next few years. I'm very doubtful about that. There are so many safety rules to deal with. Marcus: Mm. I did agree that town centres will become more about leisure, though, cafes, gyms, that kind of thing. Anya: Yes, that's already happening in our town. Marcus: It is. The old department store on the high street is being turned into a climbing centre, apparently. Anya: Really? I'd never have imagined that ten years ago. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Marcus: I found the part about different types of shops really interesting. Take supermarkets. You'd think they couldn't get any bigger, but there are more of them than ever, and they're far more efficient than they used to be, with self-checkouts and automatic stock control. Anya: Yes. And coffee shops. The number of them has grown enormously in the last twenty years. Marcus: That's because people have more money to spend on small luxuries like that. A coffee used to be something you made at home. Anya: Bookshops were surprising too. Everyone expected them to disappear when online shopping took off, but the ones that have survived have changed a lot. The staff now run author events and reading groups, and they give personal recommendations. It must be a much more interesting job than it used to be. Marcus: Definitely. What about butchers? Anya: That was quite shocking. The number of independent butchers has fallen dramatically, because most people buy their meat in supermarkets now. Marcus: And charity shops were the opposite. The lecturer thought there'll be a big rise in demand for second-hand clothes over the next few years, as people become more concerned about waste. Anya: I think she's right about that. Lots of my friends buy second-hand now. Marcus: Me too. And some charity shops are becoming quite specialised, selling only books or furniture, for example. Anya: That's true. There's one near the station that only sells books and records. Marcus: And then banks. So many branches have closed already, and I'd say most of the ones that are left are in real danger, now that nearly everyone banks online. Anya: I agree. My local branch closed last year. So, shall we use some of these examples in our presentation? Marcus: Good idea. Anya: We could start with the history, and then move on to the different types of shop. I'll look for some old photographs of the high street to show how much it's changed. Marcus: Great. And I'll find some up-to-date figures, so we're not relying only on what the lecturer said. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture on the need for a global system to track fishing vessels. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: In today's lecture, I'm going to talk about illegal fishing, and the need for an effective system to monitor fishing vessels around the world. Illegal fishing is thought to account for a significant share of the fish caught globally each year. It threatens fish populations, damages marine ecosystems and takes income away from fishing communities that follow the rules. Some estimates suggest that as much as one in five fish caught in the wild may have been taken illegally, although exact figures are, of course, very hard to obtain. Lecturer: In principle, what we need is similar to air traffic control, but for ships. We would need a system that combined international laws with digital tools that could show us, at any moment, where every fishing vessel was and what it was doing. At present, however, no such system works effectively. So what are the problems? Lecturer: Well, most large vessels are required to carry a transmitter that regularly broadcasts their position. The trouble is that these devices can easily be switched off, and some vessels do exactly that when they enter areas where fishing is not allowed. This is known as going dark. These transmitters were originally introduced to prevent collisions between ships, not to monitor fishing, which is one reason why the rules about them are not always strictly enforced. Lecturer: Another problem is that many vessels are registered in countries that have little interest in checking what they do. Owners can choose to sail under the flags of these countries, which makes it much harder to hold them responsible for breaking the rules. Lecturer: Illegal catches can also be hidden. Instead of bringing their fish to port, where it might be inspected, some fishing boats transfer their catch to larger refrigerated ships far out at sea. The fish is then mixed with legally caught fish, and it's almost impossible to trace. Some of these refrigerated ships stay at sea for months at a time, collecting fish from many different boats. Lecturer: And it isn't only large vessels we need to think about. There are millions of small fishing boats around the world, and most of them don't carry transponders at all, so they're very difficult to monitor. Lecturer: Even when information exists, it's not always shared. Some fishing companies are unwilling to reveal where their vessels operate for competitive reasons, because they don't want rivals to find out where the best fishing grounds are. And collecting the right information isn't easy. To identify illegal activity, you need to know not just a vessel's position but also its identity: who owns it, and whether it has a licence to fish in that area. Lecturer: Where vessels have gone dark, scientists can't follow them directly. What they can do is study patterns in the movements of other vessels, together with satellite images, to estimate where a missing vessel is likely to be and what it's probably doing. Lecturer: So, what solutions have been suggested? First, countries need to agree on common standards for the way information about vessels is recorded, so that data from different sources can be compared. Then this information needs to be brought together. Some organisations have already created an online map that combines data from many sources and makes it freely available, so that anyone can see where fishing is taking place. Of course, technology alone can't solve the problem, and any solution will also depend on political will. Lecturer: Finally, any global system will only work if countries are willing to take part. That means it must build confidence among governments, fishing companies and local communities that the information will be used fairly. Poorer coastal countries, in particular, often lack the patrol boats needed to act on the information, so they will also need practical support. One promising example of this that I'd like to look at now comes from West Africa. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

Ollie: The other thing I'd warn people about is relying on your phone to find your way. The battery can run out, and in the mountains there's often no signal, so always carry a paper map and a compass, and know how to use them. People sometimes ask whether they should camp alone. If you're experienced, I think that's fine, but you must tell someone where you're going. Ollie: There are also a lot of myths about wild camping. Many people believe you need expensive equipment, but that isn't true. You can start with fairly basic gear. What does matter is keeping warm, and here's something that surprises people: if you're cold at night, it's usually not because your sleeping bag isn't warm enough, but because you haven't got a good enough mat underneath you. The cold ground takes the heat from your body. Ollie: People also ask me whether wild camping is legal. The rules vary, but it is permitted in some parts of the country, such as large areas of Scotland, as long as you follow the guidelines. And please don't cook inside your tent, whatever the weather. It's very dangerous. Finally, a lot of people worry about animals attacking their tent at night. That's extremely unlikely. The worst you'll probably get is a curious sheep. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Ollie: Choosing where to camp is really important. People often tell you to look for a sheltered spot, or to avoid valleys, and there's some truth in that. But the most important thing, in my view, is to arrive at your site well before dark, so you can see the ground properly and choose a flat, dry place for your tent. Ollie: If you're a complete beginner, I wouldn't recommend relying on a guidebook, even mine, or on the camping apps you can download. The best way to start is to go on an organised trip with an experienced leader. You'll learn far more that way, and you'll be safe. Ollie: Wild camping depends on leaving the countryside exactly as you found it. You should never light a fire unless it's clearly allowed, and you must take all of your rubbish home with you, including food waste like banana skins, which take a surprisingly long time to break down. Ollie: Sadly, some popular areas have now introduced restrictions on wild camping. That isn't because of the risk of fires, although that is a concern, and it isn't to protect nesting birds. The main reason is that the number of people visiting these areas has increased enormously in recent years, and the damage caused by so many tents has become a real problem. Ollie: A word about storing food. Foxes and even cows can be surprisingly interested in your supplies, so keep your food in a sealed box outside the tent, rather than inside where you're sleeping. And never leave it lying around in open bags. Ollie: Finally, once you've got some experience, do explore new areas. But before you set off, plan your route carefully on a map, so you know where you can find water and how to get back quickly if the weather changes. Right, I'd now like to talk about some of my favourite places to camp. Some of my best memories are of places I'd never heard of until I looked closely at a map. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Anya and Marcus, discussing a seminar on the history of shopping and the future of the high street. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Marcus: That seminar on the history of shopping was really interesting, wasn't it? I'd never thought about how recent some of the things we take for granted are. Anya: I know. I didn't realise that the first self-service grocery store only opened in 1916. Before that, you had to ask a shop assistant for everything, and they'd fetch it from behind the counter. Marcus: Yes, and it completely changed the relationship between customers and shopkeepers. Suddenly people could pick things up, look at them and compare prices themselves. Anya: Exactly. And it's not surprising the idea caught on so quickly. It was faster for customers, and the shops needed fewer staff, so prices came down. Marcus: True. I thought the lecturer was a bit unfair, though, when she said they were the start of the decline of the traditional high street. Anya: Maybe. Anyway, the second half, about the future of shopping, was very optimistic, wasn't it? Marcus: Too optimistic, I'd say. She claimed that within ten years almost all shopping will be done online. I just can't see that. People still enjoy going to the shops, especially for clothes. Anya: I agree. And that idea of most deliveries being made by drones in the next few years. I'm very doubtful about that. There are so many safety rules to deal with. Marcus: Mm. I did agree that town centres will become more about leisure, though, cafes, gyms, that kind of thing. Anya: Yes, that's already happening in our town. Marcus: It is. The old department store on the high street is being turned into a climbing centre, apparently. Anya: Really? I'd never have imagined that ten years ago. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Marcus: I found the part about different types of shops really interesting. Take supermarkets. You'd think they couldn't get any bigger, but there are more of them than ever, and they're far more efficient than they used to be, with self-checkouts and automatic stock control. Anya: Yes. And coffee shops. The number of them has grown enormously in the last twenty years. Marcus: That's because people have more money to spend on small luxuries like that. A coffee used to be something you made at home. Anya: Bookshops were surprising too. Everyone expected them to disappear when online shopping took off, but the ones that have survived have changed a lot. The staff now run author events and reading groups, and they give personal recommendations. It must be a much more interesting job than it used to be. Marcus: Definitely. What about butchers? Anya: That was quite shocking. The number of independent butchers has fallen dramatically, because most people buy their meat in supermarkets now. Marcus: And charity shops were the opposite. The lecturer thought there'll be a big rise in demand for second-hand clothes over the next few years, as people become more concerned about waste. Anya: I think she's right about that. Lots of my friends buy second-hand now. Marcus: Me too. And some charity shops are becoming quite specialised, selling only books or furniture, for example. Anya: That's true. There's one near the station that only sells books and records. Marcus: And then banks. So many branches have closed already, and I'd say most of the ones that are left are in real danger, now that nearly everyone banks online. Anya: I agree. My local branch closed last year. So, shall we use some of these examples in our presentation? Marcus: Good idea. Anya: We could start with the history, and then move on to the different types of shop. I'll look for some old photographs of the high street to show how much it's changed. Marcus: Great. And I'll find some up-to-date figures, so we're not relying only on what the lecturer said. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture on the need for a global system to track fishing vessels. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: In today's lecture, I'm going to talk about illegal fishing, and the need for an effective system to monitor fishing vessels around the world. Illegal fishing is thought to account for a significant share of the fish caught globally each year. It threatens fish populations, damages marine ecosystems and takes income away from fishing communities that follow the rules. Some estimates suggest that as much as one in five fish caught in the wild may have been taken illegally, although exact figures are, of course, very hard to obtain. Lecturer: In principle, what we need is similar to air traffic control, but for ships. We would need a system that combined international laws with digital tools that could show us, at any moment, where every fishing vessel was and what it was doing. At present, however, no such system works effectively. So what are the problems? Lecturer: Well, most large vessels are required to carry a transmitter that regularly broadcasts their position. The trouble is that these devices can easily be switched off, and some vessels do exactly that when they enter areas where fishing is not allowed. This is known as going dark. These transmitters were originally introduced to prevent collisions between ships, not to monitor fishing, which is one reason why the rules about them are not always strictly enforced. Lecturer: Another problem is that many vessels are registered in countries that have little interest in checking what they do. Owners can choose to sail under the flags of these countries, which makes it much harder to hold them responsible for breaking the rules. Lecturer: Illegal catches can also be hidden. Instead of bringing their fish to port, where it might be inspected, some fishing boats transfer their catch to larger refrigerated ships far out at sea. The fish is then mixed with legally caught fish, and it's almost impossible to trace. Some of these refrigerated ships stay at sea for months at a time, collecting fish from many different boats. Lecturer: And it isn't only large vessels we need to think about. There are millions of small fishing boats around the world, and most of them don't carry transponders at all, so they're very difficult to monitor. Lecturer: Even when information exists, it's not always shared. Some fishing companies are unwilling to reveal where their vessels operate for competitive reasons, because they don't want rivals to find out where the best fishing grounds are. And collecting the right information isn't easy. To identify illegal activity, you need to know not just a vessel's position but also its identity: who owns it, and whether it has a licence to fish in that area. Lecturer: Where vessels have gone dark, scientists can't follow them directly. What they can do is study patterns in the movements of other vessels, together with satellite images, to estimate where a missing vessel is likely to be and what it's probably doing. Lecturer: So, what solutions have been suggested? First, countries need to agree on common standards for the way information about vessels is recorded, so that data from different sources can be compared. Then this information needs to be brought together. Some organisations have already created an online map that combines data from many sources and makes it freely available, so that anyone can see where fishing is taking place. Of course, technology alone can't solve the problem, and any solution will also depend on political will. Lecturer: Finally, any global system will only work if countries are willing to take part. That means it must build confidence among governments, fishing companies and local communities that the information will be used fairly. Poorer coastal countries, in particular, often lack the patrol boats needed to act on the information, so they will also need practical support. One promising example of this that I'd like to look at now comes from West Africa. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
